newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Thai-Cambodian border trade resumes after hiatus.
newsitem.headline: Thai-Cambodian border trade resumes after hiatus.

text.p: A caravan of 500 cars carried about 1,000 businessmen and Thai officials to this gem-rich town on Saturday to reopen border trade which had been halted by the United Nations in 1993.

The governor of Thailand's Chantaburi province, who led the team of businessmen to explore trade opportunties, said business should resume because the Khmer Rouge guerrillas in this region had disbanded and merged with the Phnom Penh government.

"We organised this rally and caravan to Pailin to encourage the Thai businessmen and investors that after they (Khmer Rouge)..merged with the government, Pailin is safe and good place to invest," said Amorn Anantachai.
Hundreds of Cambodian and Thai traders joined in the opening ceremony even though there were not many goods for sale yet.

"The relations between the two towns are more important than anything, so...I promise to extend my full cooperation with the Thais for border trade or whatever," Ie Chian, the governor of Pailin and former guerrilla commander of the region, told Reuters.
Pailin used to be the economic hub for the Khmer Rouge guerrillas until border trade was banned with Thailand by the United Nations Transitional Administration for Cambodia (UNTAC) in early 1993.
UNTAC accused the rebels of raping the region's natural resources, then selling logs and gems to Thai businessmen to buy weapons to use in fighting against Phnom Penh.

There are no official records of how much the Khmer Rouge use to earn from the cross-border trade but a member of the Chantaburi Chamber of Commerce estimated the Khmer Rouge made at least one billion baht ($38.5 million) a month.
Pailin has boomed since the Khmer Rouge in this region gave up the fight and joined the government last year.
"The population has increased very fast," said Lock Rat, assistant to the Pailin governor.

He said thousands of people from Batambang and other neighbouring villages have moved to Pailin in the past six months. Hundreds of new houses were seen during a visit on Saturday and dozens of others were being constructed.

"The business is very good after we ended the armed struggle to be part of the Cambodian government," said Long Gi, 44, a former guerrillas who lost one leg during the war and is now running a guest house.

More than one million Cambodians were killed by execution, starvation or malaria during the Khmer Rouge reign of terror from April 1975 to January 1979. Although the Khmer Rouge signed a United Nations peace accord, the guerrillas continued a guerrilla war against Phnom Penh.
The Khmer Rouge was weakened last year when Ieng Sary, the former foreign minister during the Khmer Rouge government, led thousands of guerrillas to split from hardline leader Pol Pot.
